en: The Contemplation on Returning to the Source through the Exhaustion of Delusion, Explaining the Profound Purport of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, composed by the Śramaṇa Fazang, Translator of Scriptures at Dajianfu Monastery of the Tang Dynasty.
Now, the Perfect Teaching is inconceivable; within a single speck of dust, it manifests all at once. The Perfect School is unfathomable; upon beholding a mere...
Though the finest hairs are displayed in uniformity,
when applied to the differentiation of substance, there is no lack of a tendency toward distinction;
as phenomena rely on principle to manifest, they naturally possess a form of ultimate unity.
It is like medicine arising when illness breaks out, and wisdom being established through the production of delusion;
when the illness is delusive, the medicine is likewise delusive, like raising an empty fist to stop a child’s crying.
When the mind is penetrating, the Dharma is penetrating, like drawing upon empty space to demonstrate its pervasiveness.
Once awakened and enlightened, what is there to be obstructed and what to be penetrated?

The hundred negations cease their攀緣 (pān-yuán, clinging to objects), and the four propositions are cut off from increase and decrease. Thus, medicine and illness both vanish together; stillness and turbulence are fused as one. By dissolving the subject-object duality, one enters the Profound Mystery; by merging nature and characteristics, one returns to the Dharma-realm.

I humbly observe that the profound framework is vast and expansive, while its subtle purport is rarefied and elusive. Those who peruse it find it difficult to exhaust its source; those who seek it rarely reach its ultimate limit. Consequently, true emptiness stagnates within the mind, constantly becoming a field for discursive thought;
the ultimate reality resides before one's eyes, yet conversely becomes a realm of names and signs.

Now, he has comprehensively gathered the profound mysteries and encompassed the great tradition; he brings forth the sūtra scrolls from within the dust and turns the wheel of Dharma upon a single hair.
For the enlightened, their virtue flourishes in this very day;
for the ignorant, their hope is severed for many lifetimes.
Those who grasp the essential intent may find even mountains and peaks easily moved;
those who deviate from the fundamental principle will find it difficult to enter [the truth] by even a grain or a hair.

Having thus repeatedly consulted the ancient edicts and scrutinized the old statutes, I have fully prepared the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka and relied upon the subtle principles of the Five Vehicles. Redundant words have been excised, and deficient meanings have been restored to their completeness.

Although this initial compilation may seem uncertain, it is all the more so justified by the existence of prior precedents. Having exhausted the ocean of this nature and assembled the forest of those practices, I have separately set forth six gates to form a single contemplation. These elements are integrated without confusion, appearing as a single, radiant horizon. I hope that those who have lost their way will return to the right path, their minds becoming clear like the rising sun; may the gentlemen who cherish the Way look down upon this with detailed scrutiny.
Now, this contemplation will be briefly elucidated by dividing it into six sections:
first, the enumeration of the names;
second, the detailed analysis.
First, manifesting the single essence, which refers to the essence of self-nature purity and perfect luminosity.
Second, giving rise to two functions:
the first is the function of the ocean-seal’s constant abiding of the myriad phenomena; the second is the function of the wondrous mirror’s successive reflection of forms.
Second, the sovereign function of the perfect clarity of the dharma-realm.
Third, the manifestation of three kinds of pervasiveness:
first, the pervasiveness of a single atom throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Second, the pervasiveness of generating the inexhaustible from a single atom;
third, the pervasiveness of containing both emptiness and existence within a single atom.
These are the four practices and four virtues:
First, the virtue of wondrous and unimpeded application according to conditions;
second, the virtue of maintaining dignified deportment with established rules;
third, the virtue of gathering and sustaining sentient beings through gentleness, flexibility, and straightforwardness.
Fourth is the merit of universally taking upon oneself the suffering of sentient beings.
Fifth is the entry into the five types of cessation (*śamatha*):
first, the cessation of illuminating the purity and emptiness of phenomena while remaining detached from conditions.
Second, the cessation of observing people’s stillness and the severance of desire;
third, the cessation of the spontaneous arising of phenomena as their inherent nature;
fourth, the cessation of the manifestation of the light of concentration through non-thought.
Fifth, the profound penetration of phenomena and principle, which is the cessation of signs.
Sixth, the cultivation of six contemplations:
first, the contemplation of true emptiness that subsumes objects within the mind;
Second, the contemplation on the wondrous existence of objects manifested from the mind;
third, the contemplation on the secret, perfect fusion of mind and object;
fourth, the contemplation on the manifestation of the reflection of wisdom within various conditions.
Fifth, the contemplation of many bodies entering into a single objective image;
sixth, the contemplation of the Indra’s Net where the principal and its attendants manifest one another.
First, regarding the manifestation of the single essence: this refers to the essence of intrinsic purity and perfect luminosity.

However, this is precisely the essence of the *dharmatā* within the *tathāgatagarbha*; from the very beginning, its nature has been spontaneously fulfilled. It remains unstained even when amidst defilement and unpurified even through cultivation; therefore, it is called "naturally pure" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).
The essence of its nature shines universally, illuminating all without exception; therefore, it is called "perfectly luminous" (*yuanming*).

Furthermore, when following the flow [of samsara], it is defiled yet remains unstained; when reversing the flow to eliminate defilement, it is not rendered pure. Thus, it may reside within the body of a sage without increasing, and dwell within the body of an ordinary person without decreasing.
Although there is a distinction between being hidden and manifest, there is no difference in their essential nature.
When obscured by afflictions, it is hidden; when realized through wisdom, it is manifest.
It is not produced by a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), but is only revealed by a revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*).
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:

"The essence of True Suchness possesses great wisdom, because it has the sense of luminosity, the sense of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm, the sense of true and authentic cognition, and the sense of the intrinsically pure mind."
As explained at length therein, it is said: "The essence is intrinsically pure and perfectly luminous.
From this point downward, regarding the arising of two functions based on that essence, it means that two functions arise based on the aforementioned pure essence.
The first is the eternally abiding function of the universal array like a sea-seal (*sāgaramudrā*).
As for the "sea-seal," it refers to the original enlightenment of *tathatā*.

When delusion is exhausted and the mind is clarified, the myriad phenomena appear simultaneously; this is like the great ocean where waves arise due to the wind, yet when the wind ceases, the seawater becomes clear and transparent, and there is no phenomenon that does not manifest.
The *Awakening of Faith* states:
"It is a treasury of immeasurable merit, the ocean of the dharmatā-tathatā.
Therefore, it is called the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).
The *Sūtra* states: "The myriad phenomena of the forest and the ten thousand images are all sealed by a single Dharma.

What is called the "single Dharma" is precisely the one mind; this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas. It is the essence of the Great Universal-Characteristic Dharma-Gate of the Single Dharma-Domain (*ekadharmadhātu*). Differences exist only in reliance upon deluded thoughts; if one is free from deluded thoughts, there is only True Suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, it is called the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"Sometimes manifesting in the forms of boys or girls, or as devas, nāgas, and asuras, even up to mahoragas; according to what they delight in, he causes them all to see him. The physical forms of sentient beings are each different, and their karmic actions and voices are likewise immeasurable; all such things he is able to manifest through the majestic spiritual power of the Ocean-Seal Samādhi."
Based on this meaning, it is called the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).

Second, the sovereign function of the perfect luminosity of the Dharma-realm is the Avataṃsaka Samādhi; that is to say, by extensively cultivating the myriad practices in accordance with principle to accomplish virtue, one universally pervades the Dharma-realm and realizes Bodhi.
Regarding the term "Avataṃsaka" (Flower Ornament): flowers have the function of producing fruit, and practice has the capacity to evoke results.
Now, by relying on these phenomena to manifest the meaning, the flower is raised as a metaphor.

"Adornment" (*vyūha*) means that the practice has been perfected and the fruit is fulfilled, in accord with principle and true to reality; where both nature and characteristics have vanished and subject and object are both severed, it is manifest, brilliant, and radiant—therefore, it is called "adornment."
Truly, without conduct that flows from the Real, there is no way to accord with the Real; how could there be any conduct that adorns the Real that does not arise from the Real?

Thus, the Real encompasses the extremities of the deluded, such that there is no practice that is not cultivated; the deluded penetrate the source of the Real, such that there is no characteristic that is not quiescent. Therefore, it is said: "The Dharma-realm is perfectly luminous and its functions are sovereign."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"Adorning and purifying inconceivable lands, making offerings to all Tathāgatas, emitting boundless great radiance, and liberating sentient beings without limit; in generosity, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, and supernormal powers—in all such matters one attains mastery through the power of the Buddha’s Flower Adornment Samādhi."
Based on this meaning, it is called the Flower Adornment Samādhi (*Huayan Samādhi*).

Third, regarding the indication of the three "pervasivities" (*bian*): this refers to how, by means of the two aforementioned functions, each individual function universally pervades the entire Dharma-realm; hence, they are termed "pervasive."
Regarding the statement "threefold pervasion":
first, the single atom universally pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
This means that the atom has no self-nature and is established by apprehending the Truth; since the Truth is boundless, the atom likewise follows suit.
The Sūtra says:

"Within every single atom of all the Flower Treasury Worlds, one perceives the entire Dharma-realm; the radiant jewels manifest Buddhas gathered like clouds—this is the Tathāgata’s mastery over his buddha-field."
Based on this principle, one should know that a single atom universally pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Second, a single atom gives rise to an inexhaustible pervasiveness.

This means that atoms have no self-nature; their arising must necessarily depend upon the Truth (tathatā). Since True Suchness possesses myriad virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the functions arising from that Truth likewise manifest in ten thousand variations.
The *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states:

"As for True Suchness (*tathatā*), its essential nature possesses the meanings of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; it possesses the meanings of being cool, unchanging, and sovereign; and it is fully endowed with merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges, such that there is not even the slightest deficiency."
The *Sūtra* states:

"Within this Flower Treasury World-Ocean, whether it be mountains, rivers, or even trees, forests, atoms, or hairs, there is not a single place that does not accord with the *dharmadhātu* of *tathatā* and possess boundless virtues."

Based on this principle, one should know that a single atom is simultaneously principle and phenomenon, person and dharma, that and this, the dependent and the primary, defilement and purity, cause and fruit, identity and difference, unity and multiplicity, vastness and narrowness, sentient and non-sentient; thus, the three bodies are identical to the ten bodies.

Why is this? Because principle and phenomena are unimpeded, and phenomena and phenomena are unimpeded; for such is the nature of dharmas, and because the ten bodies function with sovereign mastery in mutual interpenetration—this is the realm of the Universal Eye alone.
Within these aforementioned phenomena, each and every one mutually contains and encompasses the others, each possessing a realm of infinite, layered profundity.
As the *Sūtra* says:

"The inexhaustible ocean of all dharma-gates converges within the site of enlightenment of a single dharma; such is the nature of reality taught by the Buddha, which the eye of wisdom can clearly perceive through these skillful means."
Question: "According to what has been said, then upon every single atom, principle is not unmanifest, phenomena are not unfused, texts are not unexplained, and meanings are not unpenetrated."
How may those who study at this time awaken to and penetrate the realm of sensory objects so as to suddenly resolve all doubts?
Furthermore, regarding a single particle of dust, what is it that constitutes defilement?
What is called "pure"?
What constitutes the "true"?
And what is termed the "conventional"?
What is called birth-and-death?
What is called nirvana?
And what is called affliction?
What is called bodhi? What is called the Hīnayāna dharma?
What is called the Mahāyāna dharma?
"I pray you will grant me an explanation, for I have heard what I have never heard before! He replied:

"Great wisdom is perfectly luminous; it perceives a single hair-tip and yet encompasses the entire ocean of nature. The true source shines forth clearly; it dwells within a single speck of dust and yet illuminates the entire body."
The arising of the myriad dharmas must be simultaneous and of one boundary; in principle, there is no sequence of before and after. Why is this?
Because this single speck of dust, as a false appearance, is able to obscure the Truth, which is precisely what constitutes defilement.
Because these phenomenal marks of the dust are empty and non-existent, they are "purity" (śuddha).
Because the fundamental nature of these dusts is identical to Suchness (tathatā), it is "reality" (bhūta).
Because these phenomenal marks of the dust arise through conditions as illusory existence, it is "conventionality" (saṃvṛti).
Because the characteristics of sensory objects undergo transformation and change from moment to moment, they are birth and death.
Because one contemplates that the arising and ceasing of these characteristics are ultimately empty and devoid of reality, this is nirvana.
The large and small characteristics of sensory objects are all the conceptual discriminations of the deluded mind, which are themselves afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because the essence of these sensory characteristics is fundamentally empty and quiescent, when objective consideration naturally ceases, this is itself awakening (*bodhi*).
The absence of the intrinsic nature of objective phenomena through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) is the Dharma of the Hīnayāna.
The non-arising and non-ceasing of the nature of objective phenomena, which exist as dependent appearances (*paratantra*), is the Dharma of the Mahāyāna.

This has been explained in brief; were it to be stated in full, even if all sentient beings, each harboring different doubts, were to ask the Tathāgata simultaneously, the Tathāgata would explain them using only the single character "dust" (reṇu). You should reflect upon this deeply.
The *Sūtra* says: "The inexhaustible ocean of all dharma-gates is fully expounded by a single word, leaving nothing behind.
Based on this meaning, it is called "the production from a single atom of the inexhaustible and all-pervading."
Third, a single atom contains both emptiness and existence pervasively.
This means that because the atom lacks intrinsic nature, it is empty; yet because its illusory appearance is vividly present, it is existent.
This is truly because illusory form has no substance and thus is not different from emptiness, while true emptiness possesses all virtues and penetrates beyond the realm of existence.
To contemplate form as emptiness is to achieve great wisdom and not abide in birth-and-death;
to contemplate emptiness as form is to achieve great compassion and not abide in nirvana.
Only when form and emptiness are non-dual, and compassion and wisdom are indistinguishable, does one attain the ultimate reality.
The *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:
"Before attaining the Way, bodhisattvas still harbor three doubts regarding this wondrous existence within true emptiness:
first, they doubt that emptiness annihilates form, thereby grasping at a nihilistic emptiness."
Second, they doubt that emptiness is distinct from form and grasp at emptiness as being external to form.
Third, they doubt that emptiness is a substantial entity and grasp at emptiness as something existent.
This commentary now explains: form is illusory form and necessarily does not obstruct emptiness; emptiness is true emptiness and necessarily does not obstruct form.
If it were obstructed by form, it would be empty annihilation; if it were obstructed by emptiness, it would be substantial form.
Since even a single atom possesses the aforementioned wondrous existence within true emptiness, one should know that every atom and so forth is likewise so.

If one realizes this principle, then the sensory objects will contain the ten directions without any impairment to their magnitude or minuteness, and mindfulness will encompass the nine periods of time such that extension and brevity are simultaneous. Thus, the sublime and subtle words manifest even a single hair’s breadth within the Perfect Teaching, and the wondrous assembly of sages appears as a mere speck of dust within the entire body; it utterly transcends the limits of speech and thought, and breaks through the confines of all conceptual nets.
The Sūtra says: "Suppose there were a great sūtra scroll, equal in size to the three thousandfold world system, contained within a single mote of dust; and so it is with every mote of dust."
"There was a wise person whose pure eyes saw clearly everywhere; he broke through the dust to reveal the scripture, extensively benefiting sentient beings," and so forth.

According to the underlying principle, this means that sentient beings within the dust delusively conceptualize the scripture as the perfect clarity of great wisdom (*mahājñāna*). Since the essence of this wisdom is boundless, it is said that its measure is equal to the three thousandfold world-system.
Based on this meaning, it is said that "a single atom contains both emptiness and existence and pervades all.

From here below, one practices the four virtues based on this pervasive object; that is, based on the aforementioned object of a single atom that is able to pervade, one cultivates the four kinds of virtuous practices.
First is the virtue of wondrous and unimpeded function according to conditions.
This means that based on the Truth (*tathatā*), one gives rise to function to extensively benefit all sentient beings.

Since the faculties and capacities of sentient beings are unequal, their modes of reception and understanding differ in myriad ways, and their inclinations and desires vary, one bestows the Dharma in accordance with their capacities and administers medicine according to their ailments so that they may take it up and practice it; this meaning is fully elucidated in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
Furthermore, because of great compassion, it is called "following conditions";
because of great wisdom, it is called "sublime function";
and furthermore, while utterly destroying provisional names, it constantly delivers sentient beings.
Therefore it is said: To know through following conditions that the nature of sentient beings is empty, such that in reality there is no one who delivers them, is called "wondrous function.
Furthermore, because principle is identical to phenomena, it is called "following conditions"; because phenomena are identical to principle, it is called "wondrous function.
Moreover, because the true does not contradict the conventional, it is "following conditions"; because the conventional does not contradict the true, it is "wondrous function."

Furthermore, because it arises from the fundamental to manifest as the derivative, it accords with conditions; because it gathers the derivative back into the fundamental, it constitutes wondrous function.

This is truly because the Dharma has no boundaries: arising necessarily occurs simultaneously. True Reality does not obstruct the myriad differences, and its manifestations respond such that nothing is not of one single limit. When functioning, it surges like boiling waves, operating entirely through the movement of the true essence;
when abiding in essence, it is like a mirror’s purity or still water, wherein every accord with conditions converges into quiescence.
Like the radiance of the sun's rays, it illuminates the ten directions without conscious intent;
like a clear mirror reflecting forms, it manifests myriad images without movement.
Therefore, it is said that its wondrous function follows conditions, its virtue being boundless.
Second is the virtue of abiding in proper deportment with established rules.
This refers to the four modes of conduct: walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.

The eighty thousand [precepts] of the Mahāyāna and the three thousand [precepts] of the Hīnayāna serve as the model for maintaining these practices. They rectify the disordered threads of the six harmonies, provide the ladder for ascending beyond the triple world, and act as the swift vessel for crossing the ocean of suffering. For rescuing beings and guiding the deluded, nothing is superior to this.

However, because the golden countenance has hidden its luster and the True Teaching has declined, the transmission has become corrupted as teachers follow their own subjective views. Consequently, the teachings lack discipline; people indiscriminately draw from the pure stream, treating gain and loss as equal and falsely conflating the mundane with the true and pure. Thus, beginners commit errors at every turn, failing to rely on the Sūtras and Vinaya, confusing ordinary sentiments, and sinking both themselves and others—this is truly pitiable.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Neither sinking too deeply nor floating too lightly, one should always abide in the fundamental retinue of right mindfulness and purely cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*)."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"Precepts are the foundation of unsurpassed bodhi; one should fully maintain pure precepts.
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:
"By means of this, the multitude of subtle-dust bodhisattvas attain perfect enlightenment. The *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states:

"Because one knows that the essence of the dharma-nature is beyond the violation of precepts, one accordingly practices the śīla-pāramitā in accordance with the dharma-nature. This refers to not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, and not speaking falsely; it involves distancing oneself from greed, anger, deceit, flattery, and false views. One should also distance oneself from clamor and distraction, possessing few desires and being content, even feeling great dread toward minor transgressions. One must not treat lightly the prohibitions and precepts established by the Tathāgata, constantly guarding against censure and ensuring that sentient beings do not give rise to faults or offenses through delusion."
"By means of these modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), one abides and sustains [the Dharma] in order to transform sentient beings.
Question:

"According to what was explained above, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is of a single characteristic, the Buddha-body is non-dual, and it is replete with all merits; for what reason, then, is it necessary to have modes of deportment and other forms of ethical conduct (*śīla*)?"
He replied:
"Suppose, for example, there is a great maṇi jewel whose essential nature is luminous and pure, yet which has long been burdened by dust and accumulation, resulting in coarse and filthy stains.
If a person merely contemplates the nature of the jewel but does not subject it to various forms of polishing and treatment, it will never become pure."
The dharma-body of True Suchness (tathatā) is by nature empty and pure, yet it has long been defiled by the stains of ignorance and afflictions.
If a person merely contemplates True Suchness without cultivating it through various practices such as ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, it will never become purified.
"Based on this principle, it is logically necessary to uphold the precepts. Question:
"The five groups of monastics have transcended the secular world and may thus fully possess dignified deportment."
"Those who dwell at home are entangled in the worldly net; how could they be free from transgressions?
He replied:
"The class of those who have left the home life has its own strict precepts, whereas those who remain at home generally observe the five precepts."

Now, the Three Refuges and Five Precepts are truly the bridge for crossing the sea of suffering, the foundation for proceeding toward Nirvana, the preliminary stage for the Vinaya, and the noble basis for the seven classes of disciples. All myriad virtues arise by depending upon them; they are indeed the level ground of the Buddha-dharma.
The Sūtra says: "If śīla is not pure, samādhi will not manifest.
One should know that śīla is the substance of concentration, while prajñā is its function; when the three trainings are perfected, one realizes bodhi.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:

"First, one upholds the precepts without violation; the bhikṣu’s deportment is naturally dignified and majestic. Enemies cannot approach him, yet if he acts contrary to the Dharma, he will be rebuked."
Based on this principle, it is said that there is the virtue of maintaining dignified deportment with regularity.
Third is the virtue of gathering in sentient beings through gentleness and straightforwardness.
This means that great wisdom illuminating reality is called "straightforwardness," while great compassion rescuing all things is called "gentleness."
Furthermore, "uprightness" refers to the non-deviation from one's fundamental nature;

"gentleness and harmony" refer to the absence of stagnation while following the flow of conditions. Gentleness serves to subdue and extinguish afflictions, while harmony serves to practice in accordance with principle. By employing this method of harmonization, one gathers in and guides sentient beings.

Furthermore, as for being upright and honest (*rju*), it means that one’s nature is free from falsehood and deceit, such that one’s words and deeds correspond; one harbors virtue within the heart and is unconcerned with fame or profit, regarding gold as lightly as a clod of earth and valuing the teachings more than any treasure. Acting solely for the sake of right livelihood and the harmonious development of beings, one swiftly aspires to the perfection of both self and others; therefore, this is called the virtue of gathering beings through gentleness, uprightness, and honesty.
Fourth is the merit of universally taking the suffering of sentient beings upon oneself.

This means practicing various dharmas not for one's own sake, but solely with the desire to extensively benefit all living beings—whether enemies or kin—with impartiality, so that they may universally sever evil, fully cultivate the myriad practices, and swiftly realize Bodhi.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva’s great compassion and great vow take his own body as collateral; he rescues all sentient beings suffering in the three evil realms, ensuring they attain happiness, with a mind that never falters until the end of the future, yet he harbors not even a hair’s breadth of hope for a reward from those beings.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"A vast cloud of compassion pervades all things; he has sacrificed his body as many times as there are atoms in immeasurable lands. By the power of his practice throughout oceans of past eons, this world is now free from all defilements."
This means that sentient beings falsely cling to the constant flux of every thought-moment and designate it as "suffering";
the Bodhisattva teaches them to realize that the aggregates are empty and quiescent, and that their intrinsic nature is fundamentally non-existent, and thus speaks of "being free from suffering."
Question:
"Sentient beings are infinite, and their suffering and karma are infinite; how can a bodhisattva universally take upon themselves the suffering of sentient beings? Answer:

"When a Bodhisattva undergoes suffering on behalf of sentient beings, it is due to the power of great compassion and skillful means; yet because sentient beings cling to false attachments and do not understand that the essence of karma arises from delusion, they have no way to escape suffering."

The Bodhisattva instructs others to cultivate the two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* without the mind wavering for even a moment; thus, causes and effects are extinguished, and suffering karma has no basis from which to arise. Merely ensuring that beings do not enter the three miserable realms is called the "merit of universally taking the suffering of sentient beings upon oneself."
The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* states:
"Perceiving the non-substantial as substantial, dwelling deeply in perversion, and being free from the afflictions that cause distress, one attains supreme enlightenment."
The above concludes the clarification of the four kinds of virtuous practices.
From here on, the application is subsumed within the essence as one enters the five gates of cessation (*śamatha*).

As for these five gates of cessation: it means that by relying on the aforementioned practices of the four virtues, one cultivates cessation through the realization that the very characteristics [of phenomena] are empty; thus, when characteristics are exhausted, the mind becomes tranquil.

As for what is called "entering," it means that both nature and characteristics are utterly extinguished, and the essence pervades the entire Dharma-realm; entering while being devoid of the characteristic of entering is what is meant by "entering.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"The profound realm of the Tathāgata is equal in measure to empty space; all sentient beings enter it, yet in reality there is nothing entered."
Furthermore, according to the *Buddhaviṣayāvatāra-sūtra*:
"Entering into the various signless concentrations (*animitta-samādhi*), one perceives the tranquility of all phenomena.
Because one constantly enters into equanimity, I pay homage to that which is without an object of observation."
This means that all sentient beings are from the very beginning nowhere outside the realm of the Tathāgata; there is nothing further to enter.
It is like a person who, due to delusion, mistakes the east for the west;
yet once they have awakened, the west is simply the east, and there is no other east to enter.
Because sentient beings are deluded, they claim that the false can be abandoned and that the true can be entered;
yet even upon awakening, the false is itself the true, and there is no separate truth to be entered.
This principle is likewise: though there is no entering, it is called "entering" because one enters.
Why is this? Because entering and non-entering are fundamentally equal, being of one single Dharma-realm.
The *Awakening of Faith* states:
"If there are sentient beings who are able to contemplate non-thought, this is called entering the gate of True Suchness.
Regarding the five types of cessation (*śamatha*):
First is the cessation through clarity and detachment from conditions (*ālambana-viveka-vyupaśama*).

This means that the phenomena of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) are by nature empty and quiescent, while the phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), though appearing to exist, are immediately empty. Both the ultimate and the conventional are pure, vacant, and utterly free of dependence. The cognizing wisdom is tranquil and the object of cognition is empty; neither mind nor object imposes constraints, as their substance merges into a vast, open expanse. At the moment of correct realization, both causes and conditions are simultaneously transcended.
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
"Dharmas do not belong to causes, nor do they reside in conditions.
Based on this principle, it is said that the illumination of dharmas is pure and void, ceasing from conditions.
Second, observing persons as tranquil and devoid of desire through cessation.

This means that the five aggregates have no master, which is called "tranquility"; being empty and still, without seeking, is called "devoid of desire. Therefore, it is said: "observing persons as tranquil and devoid of desire through cessation."
Third, the cessation that is the natural law of the profuse arising of nature (*xingqi*).

This means that the arising of function based on the essence is called "arising from nature" (*xingqi*); because this arising responds to the myriad differences, it is termed "profuse arising"; and because this has been so at all times throughout antiquity and the present, it is called "the natural law" (*fieri*).

This means that the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā), by its very nature, accords with conditions so that the myriad dharmas arise together; it likewise returns to its nature by its very nature. Therefore, it is said: "The profuse arising of phenomena is the natural cessation within the nature."
The Sūtra says: "All dharmas are established based upon the root of non-abiding.
This is precisely its meaning.
Fourth is the cessation of non-thought manifested by the Light of Samādhi (*Samādhiprabhāsa*).

As for "the Light of Samādhi," it refers to the jewel of the *Vajra* (Ten-Thousand-Syllable) Wheel King within the White-Pure Jewel Net of the One Vehicle teaching. This jewel is, in its essential nature, transparent and luminous, illuminating the ten directions simultaneously; it accomplishes tasks without thought, and all who contemplate it follow it.
Although it manifests wondrous powers, its mind is free from discursive thought.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"For example, when a wheel-turning monarch achieves the seven supreme treasures, their place of origin cannot be found; the nature of karma is likewise."

"If there are sentient beings who enter this gate of great quiescence and wondrous contemplation, they will accomplish all tasks spontaneously, without thought or deliberation. Like that precious jewel which illuminates both near and far equally, appearing with distinct clarity and pervading the void, they cannot be obscured by the dust, mist, smoke, or clouds of the two vehicles or externalists. Therefore, it is called the manifestation of the light of concentration through non-conceptual stillness."
Fifth, the profound interpenetration of principle and phenomena, which is beyond the cessation of marks.
This means that illusory phenomena and the markless principle mutually conceal and mutually manifest one another; therefore, it is called "profound interpenetration."

Furthermore, because principle is manifested through cultivation, phenomena penetrate into principle; because practice arises from principle, principle penetrates into phenomena. As they mutually sustain and mutually negate one another, it is called "mysterious penetration."
"Profound penetration" means that great wisdom exists alone, its essence pervading the entire Dharma-realm, while great compassion rescues all beings, with myriad practices unfolding in profusion.

When compassion and wisdom are fused as one, and both nature and characteristics are extinguished, it is therefore said that "the profound penetration of principle and phenomena is the cessation of signs."
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the five types of śamatha.
From here on, based upon śamatha, one gives rise to vipaśyanā.
Question:
"Based on the principles explained above, practicing in accordance with them is sufficient for perfection; why then must one further enter the two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*?
Answer: "The *Awakening of Faith* says:..."
"If one cultivates *śamatha*, it serves as an antidote to the ordinary person's attachment to the mundane world and enables the relinquishing of the timid views of the two vehicles.

If one cultivates *vipaśyanā*, it serves as an antidote to the fault of the two vehicles' failure to give rise to great compassion and their narrow-mindedness, and it distances one from the ordinary person's failure to cultivate roots of goodness."
For this reason, the two gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā mutually support and assist one another, never being separated.
Without cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā, there is no way to enter the path to bodhi.
The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra says:

"For example, it is like the garuḍa, which flaps its left and right wings to toss the waters of the ocean, causing them to part so that it may observe the hosts of nāgas and seize those whose lives are about to end."

The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is also like this: taking great tranquility and sublime insight as his two wings, he stirs the great ocean of the waters of universal love for sentient beings, causing it to open wide so that he may observe all beings and deliver those whose faculties have matured.
"It is on account of this principle that one must cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā.

He asked: "Since the two gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā constitute the essential core, ordinary beginners do not yet understand how to settle the mind; please show the way for these deluded followers so they may return to the correct path."
Answer: According to the *Awakening of Faith*, it says:

"If one practices *śamatha* (calm abiding), one dwells in a quiet place, sits upright with a correct mind, not relying on the breath, not relying on forms or colors, not relying on space, nor on earth, water, fire, or wind, and so forth, not relying even on seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. All conceptualizations are eliminated as they arise; one also eliminates the very thought of elimination, for all phenomena are originally without conceptualization—moment by moment they do not arise, and moment by moment they do not cease. Furthermore, one does not follow the mind’s outward thoughts toward objects, and subsequently uses the mind to eliminate the mind."
"If the mind wanders and scatters, you must immediately collect it and bring it back to right mindfulness.
By constantly and diligently practicing the contemplation of mind-only consciousness through right mindfulness, all demonic realms will naturally be left behind.

Ordinary beings who are beginners have not yet distinguished between the heterodox and the orthodox; thus, the net of Māra enters their minds to deceive them. Furthermore, lacking a master from whom they may seek counsel, they have no basis for reliance. Mistaking the activities of the four Māras for the True Path, as days and months pass and their false views deepen, even if they eventually encounter a virtuous condition, it will be difficult to change them. Sunk in the sea of suffering with no means of escape, examine yourself deeply and do not allow this vigilance to falter for even a moment.
This meaning is as explained in the *Awakening of Faith*.

Sixth, regarding the arousal of the six contemplations: based on the preceding five gates, one arouses the contemplation that is "stopping while in movement," which is the contemplation within stopping.
Why is this? Because principle and phenomena are unimpeded, for such is the nature of dharmas;
because concentration and wisdom are mutually integrated, being free from all limitations.
The one and the many are mutually identical because they transcend before and after;
the great function is sovereign because it is free from obstruction.
Regarding the six contemplations: the first is the Contemplation of True Emptiness that Subsumes Objects within the Mind.
This means that all phenomena within the three realms are created solely by the one mind; since not a single dharma can be found apart from the mind, it is said that they "return to the mind.
This means that all conceptual discriminations arise only from one's own mind, and there has never been an external object outside the mind that could serve as a condition for the mind.
Why is this? Because the mind does not arise and external objects are fundamentally empty.
As the *Treatise* states:
"Because one relies on consciousness-only, and because objects fundamentally lack intrinsic nature, the meaning of true emptiness is established;
since sensory objects do not exist, the fundamental consciousness does not arise."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"As long as one has not realized that objects are mind-only, various kinds of conceptual discrimination arise; once one has realized that objects are mind-only, such discrimination no longer arises."
Knowing that all phenomena are mind-only, one abandons the appearances of external objects; thereby, through the cessation of conceptual discrimination, one awakens to the equality of true emptiness.
Just as there is a king of physicians in the world who saves the sick with wondrous medicines, so too do the Buddhas teach "mind-only" for the sake of sentient beings.
"By this one comes to know that objects manifest from the mind and the mind manifests from objects; the mind does not reach the object, nor do objects enter the mind.
One should form this contemplation. Because its wisdom is profoundly deep, it is called the 'True Emptiness Contemplation of Subsuming Objects into Mind.'"
Second is the contemplation of the wondrous existence of objects manifested from the mind.
This means that while phenomena do not obstruct the principle, differences arise according to those phenomena.

That is to say, whereas in the previous section one subsumes characteristics back into the essence, in this present section one gives rise to function based upon the essence, fully cultivating the myriad practices to adorn the land of retribution.
Furthermore, in the previous section, the characteristics were subsumed into the essence to reveal the Dharmakāya;

now, in this section, function arises based on the essence to cultivate and perfect the Saṃbhogakāya. Therefore, it is called "the contemplation of wondrous existence wherein the objective realm manifests from the mind."
Third is the contemplation of the secret, perfect fusion of mind and environment.
"Mind" refers to the unimpeded mind, which all Buddhas realize to form the Dharma-body;
"environment" refers to the unimpeded environment, which all Buddhas realize to form the Pure Land.

This refers to the fact that the Tathāgata’s reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and its supporting pure land are perfectly interfused and without obstruction; or, the body manifests as the land, as the *Sūtra* says:

"Within a single pore are immeasurable lands, each with four continents and four great oceans; Mount Sumeru and the Iron Ring Mountains are likewise present therein, all appearing within it without any crowding."
Alternatively, some lands manifest the body of a Buddha, as the *Sūtra* says:

"In every single atom of all the worlds within the Flower Treasury (*Puṣpasaṃbhava*), a Buddha enters; universally for the sake of sentient beings he performs spiritual transformations—such is the Dharma of Vairocana."
Within this section, it is divided into four propositions as explained in the *Xuantan shu* (Commentary on the Profound Introduction).

In this way, the primary environment and the sentient beings therein are interpenetrated without boundaries; whereas the preceding two contemplations each describe one side, the present [contemplation] integrates and unifies both mind and object.
Therefore, it is called the "Contemplation of the Secret, Perfectly Interpenetrating Mind and Object."
Fourth is the contemplation on the manifestation of the reflection of the body of wisdom within all conditions.

This means that while the essence of wisdom is singular and capable of mirroring all conditions, the characteristics of those conditions are fundamentally empty. The essence of wisdom illuminates quiescence; when the characteristics of all conditions are exhausted, suchness alone remains.

This means that among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), there are none that do not inherently contain true nature (*tathatā*). It is like the solar disc shining upon the vast expanse of space: those with sight can all behold it, yet even those born blind receive its moistening benefit, being made aware of the seasons and the periods of cold and heat, so that even insentient things such as grasses and trees all flourish and grow.
The sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise; therefore, it is said that the reflection of the body of wisdom appears within all conditions for observation.
Fifth is the contemplation of many bodies entering into a single mirror-image.
This is precisely the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*).
It means that the ten bodies of Vairocana function interdependently without any obstruction.
As the *Sūtra* says:

"Or they may manifest their own body as the bodies of sentient beings, the bodies of lands, the bodies of karmic retribution, the bodies of śrāvakas, the bodies of pratyekabuddhas, the bodies of bodhisattvas, the bodies of Tathāgatas, the bodies of wisdom, the bodies of Dharma, or the bodies of empty space."
In this way, any one of these ten bodies subsumes the remaining nine; therefore, it is called "the contemplation of many bodies entering into a single mirror-image.

Just as one body performs the functions of the ten bodies for one another, so too within every single pore, every single part of the body, and every single joint, all ten bodies perform their functions for one another. Sometimes the Buddha-performing activity of the ear-sense base is carried out by means of the eye-sense base, and sometimes the Buddha-performing activity of the eye-sense base is carried out by means of the ear-sense base; the same applies to the nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Why is this? Because by realizing the power of the dharmas of this great tranquility (*śamatha*) and sublime insight (*vipaśyanā*), one attains such [realization].
As the *Sūtra* says:
"Or by means of many bodies, they manifest as one body; or by means of one body, they manifest as many bodies; or they enter many bodies with one body; or they enter one body with many bodies."

It is not that one body perishes and many bodies arise, nor that many bodies perish and one body arises; all such occurrences are possible solely through the power of profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

One may enter concentration with a different object and emerge with the same object, or enter with the same object and emerge with a different object; one may enter with a single body and emerge as many bodies, or enter with many bodies and emerge as a single body. Therefore, it is said: "many bodies enter into the contemplation of a single mirror-image."
Sixth is the contemplation of the Indra’s Net of the mutual manifestation of principal and satellites.

This means that taking oneself as the principal and others as the satellites, or taking a single phenomenon as the principal and all phenomena as the satellites, or taking one body as the principal and all bodies as the satellites—whichever single phenomenon is raised, both the principal and the satellites are simultaneously encompassed. This is infinitely layered and inexhaustible; it symbolizes the nature of reality (dharmatā) manifesting in infinite layers, being entirely inexhaustible within all matters, and it also represents the inexhaustible layering of compassion and wisdom.

As it is said: "The youth Sudhana, proceeding gradually southward from the Jeta Grove, arrived before the Great Adorned Pavilion of Vairocana; there he briefly composed his mind and addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
'I pray only that the Great Sage will open the door of this pavilion so that I may enter.'"
Maitreya snapped his fingers, and the gate opened immediately.
Once Sudhana had entered, it closed again as before.

Within the pavilion, he saw hundreds of thousands of pavilions; before each pavilion stood a Maitreya Bodhisattva, and before each Maitreya Bodhisattva stood a Sudhana youth. Each of these Sudhana youths stood with palms joined in reverence before Maitreya.
This signifies that the Dharma-realm is infinitely layered, like the net of Indra, without end.
This clarifies that Sudhana, relying on this principle of the Huayan Dharma-realm, has reached the ultimate stage of his practice and attained sudden realization of the Dharma-realm.

This takes one pavilion as the principal and all other pavilions as its attendants; therefore, it is called the "Indra's Net Contemplation" of the mutual manifestation of principal and attendants, which is also the contemplation of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena.

Regarding the six successive gates of contemplation described above, one is taken as the primary and the other five as its companions; there is no fixed sequence of beginning or end, as they are all simultaneous. Upon entering any single gate, the entire Dharma-realm is fully encompassed.
This principle may be illustrated by a round pearl pierced with six holes: as soon as one enters through any single hole, the entire pearl is fully contained within. This is likewise the case here;

though opened into six gates, upon entering through any one gate, the entirety of the Dharma-realm—the perfect teachings and principles—is fully encompassed. For such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): because Sudhana realized them all completely in a single lifetime, there is no obstruction between contraction and expansion, and appearance and disappearance occur simultaneously. Within this single limit, there is no beginning or end; in its coming and going, there is no distinction between the manifest and the hidden.

At the initial awakening of the right mind, many lifetimes are subsumed within a single kṣaṇa; when the ten stages of faith are perfected, a single thought-moment encompasses the stage of Buddhahood. This causes Bodhisattvas prior to the stages to give rise to doubt regarding encountered phenomena, while the profound insight of the five hundred Śrāvakas becomes utterly beyond their reach. Through the unimpeded interpenetration of the one and the many, perfect realization and resonance constitute what is called the stage of Buddhahood.
However, the names of this contemplation gate are not fixed. If named according to its single essence, it is the Samādhi Gate of the Radiant Manifestation of the Ocean Seal;
if discussed in terms of its two functions, it is called the Samādhi Gate of the Sublime Practice of the Avataṃsaka;
and if spoken of according to its threefold pervasiveness, it is the Samādhi Gate of the Dust-Atom Containing the Ten Directions.
If named according to the four virtues, it is called the Samādhi Door of Gathering Beings through the Four Means of Integration;
if discussed in terms of the five cessations, it is the Samādhi Door of Unobstructed Quiescence and Function;
and if designated by way of the six contemplations, it is the Samādhi Door of the Unobstructed Buddha-Fruit.
Such meanings as these are established as names according to their respective virtues; based on the teachings, they are explained as the six contemplations.

By entering through a single gate, all virtues are fully possessed: since non-arising is revealed, illusory existence is not lost; the entire Dharma-realm is subsumed within a single atom, and a single body manifests as ten bodies. Meanings such as these are beyond the reach of ordinary intellect; when consciousness is exhausted and views are eliminated, they become visible through reflection.
Although I am not quick-witted, I have long cherished this sūtra; thus, I have briefly composed these "Random Wood" writings to collect its boundlessly vast meanings.
The eulogy says:
Having thoroughly investigated the foundations of all teachings, I have compiled this contemplation of the Avataṃsaka.
The phrasing is concise yet the meaning is complete; the wise should study it with diligence.

This is the *Record of the Contemplation for Returning to the Source through the Exhaustion of Delusion*, which expounds the profound purport of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Revised and re-edited twice. Composed by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui during the Song Dynasty. In the past, the Dharma Master Zhizhuan of Gushan once remarked:
"The Venerable Dushun extracted the deep purport of the *Avataṃsaka* and composed this text."
This is based on the preface by Gao Ying, Secretariat Drafter of the Tang Dynasty, to the inscription for the Northern Pagoda.
Previously, Jingyuan read the "Record of the Miaojue Pagoda" composed by the Tang Prime Minister Pei Xiu, in which the record states:

"The Master of the Avataṃsaka Commentaries revered the *Returning to the Source* (Huayan yuanren lun) of Xianshou, studying and savoring it without weariness, like a black dragon sporting with its pearls."
Thus, one knows that this commentary was indeed composed by the Venerable Master Xianshou.
Furthermore, observing that the three sections of the text are fully cited within it, all of which are the Master’s own words, they are clearly evident.

In the eleventh month of winter, the first year of the Xīníng era, I personally brought the texts from various prefectures and again requested the Great Master Tōngyì, Zǐníng, of Qiāntáng, to re-examine and revise their wording.

Master Ning was profoundly learned and possessed deep knowledge of antiquity; he diligently examined various texts, contemplating them in the morning and pondering them in the evening. He then said to Yuan:
"The words cited in the collection compiled by Master Xian-shou have been recovered through diligent rescue and recovery!"
Please allow me to set forth one or two points.
Does the *Guan* not say:
"When function is distinguished from essence, there is no lack of the potential for differentiation; when phenomena rely on principle to manifest, they naturally possess the form of ultimate unity."
"This is one of the 'One Hundred Gates of the Ocean of Meaning' (Yihai baimen).
It further states:
'To rescue beings and guide the deluded, nothing is superior to this. Is this not the preface to the *Commentary on the Heart Sutra of Prajñā*?"
Furthermore, as for the statement, "Within this section, it is divided into four propositions," this too has already been clarified in the profound discourse of the Jin commentary!
Yuan responded, saying:

"Now, when there are categories that are not disordered, it demonstrates that the net is held by its main rope; when one probes deep expressions, the value lies in their resonance with common meaning."
Thus, when a gentleman studies extensively the ancestral teachings and possesses outstanding discernment, how could this have been the case only in the past?

Yuan Ai, who transmits the ancestral teachings of Ci’en and understands the meanings of the masters, lectures on the Five Classics of the Confucianists; yet he examines the texts and seeks the reality of their meaning, clarifying their similarities and differences with a mind that accords with my own. It is for this reason that I have inscribed these words at the end of the scroll.
Completed with a second revision by Ji.
